UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



                                                             )
Western Seams Coordination                                   )                     Docket No. AD26-10-000
                                                             )


                                     COMMENTS OF
                          CORPORATE ENERGY BUYERS ASSOCIATION

Corporate Energy Buyers Association (CEBA) submits these comments regarding the California

Independent System Operator Corporation (CAISO) and the Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP)

(collectively, the Parties) Joint Report in response to the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission’s (FERC or Commission) July 16, 2026 order in this proceeding. 1 CEBA

appreciates the Parties’ reporting on the status of seams coordination in the Western

Interconnection and recognizes the work done so far. However, CEBA believes the Joint Report

does not sufficiently consider certain inefficiencies that may materialize during cross-seams trade

nor establish a pathway toward addressing these inefficiencies. As discussed herein, CEBA

recommends that the Commission require the Parties to file a supplement to the Joint Report

addressing multiple issues that are not adequately addressed in the initial filing. In the

alternative, CEBA recommends that the Commission establish a mandatory schedule for

additional filings from the Parties after both markets are in operation.




1
    CAISO & SPP, Joint Report, Docket No. AD26-10-000 (filed Sept. 30, 2026) (Joint Report).

                                                         1
 I.         INTRODUCTION

            CEBA is a business association that activates energy buyers and their partners to drive

low-cost, reliable, carbon emissions-free global energy systems. Our members represent $40

trillion in market value, including energy customers of all sizes, suppliers, and service

providers. 2 CEBA has long championed the formation of organized wholesale markets in the

West as a means to unleash the power of competition to secure reliable, low-cost energy to power

our members’ investments in communities across the West.

           CEBA has closely monitored and participated in the development of the Parties’

respective day-ahead markets in the Western Interconnection: CAISO’s Extended Day Ahead

Market (EDAM) and SPP’s Markets+. This includes current participation in the Markets+

Executive Committee, as well as prior participation in the Markets+ Seams Working Group,

Transmission Working Group, Resource Adequacy Task Force, and Rates Task Force. CEBA also

participated in the West-Wide Governance Pathways Initiative as an alternate on the Launch

Committee and as a member of the Commercial and Industrial Customer Sector. CEBA’s

engagement in the development of these markets is primarily focused on promoting structures

that facilitate efficient trade across the Western Interconnection and allow expedited

development of the resources needed to meet our members’ procurement needs.

           To this end, the Joint Report provides a valuable synopsis of key activities to date

concerning the mitigation of potential adverse impacts of market integration and cross-seams

trade. The Parties outline the various efforts undertaken by SPP and CAISO to address seams




2
    A list of current CEBA members is accessible at: https://www.ceba.org/members/.

                                                          2
 management, particularly highlighting joint efforts such as executive level meetings, staff

discussions, and public workshops.

       While this status update is valuable, the Parties have not addressed various inefficiencies

that may arise as these markets come online and cross-seams trade begins. Furthermore, the

Parties have not defined timelines under which they plan to address these concerns. CEBA

discusses these concerns in depth in the comments below.


II.    COMMENTS

       The Joint Report discusses the Parties’ commitment to coordination across market seams

and identifies a variety of efforts aimed at ensuring reliable operations among participating and

non-participating balancing authorities. However, the Joint Report largely characterizes market

seams as operational coordination challenges and gives comparatively little attention to the

economic implications of maintaining multiple adjacent market footprints. The Joint Report

points to the completed or ongoing activities related to improved communication between the

markets, enhanced data sharing and system model updates, and coordination between reliability

coordinators. While these actions are critical to grid operations, they do not address the

significant potential impact of economic inefficiencies that could arise through unmitigated

seams impacts.

       The sections below discuss the need to consider overlapping market footprints, shifting

market participation, and economic inefficiencies that are likely to occur at market seams. A

proactive plan of action is needed to address these concerns, particularly in current market

conditions, with some consideration of how experiences from the Eastern Interconnection can

inform the Parties’ mitigation strategy.



                                                 3
            a. The Joint Report Does Not Sufficiently Consider Economic Friction to Trading
              Across Seams

           The Joint Report contains extensive discussion regarding communication protocols,

stakeholder engagement, reliability coordination, and operational planning. However, the Joint

Report does not sufficiently discuss the various economic inefficiencies that may materialize

during cross-seams trade. Beyond reliability, economic efficiency is one of the primary intended

benefits of market integration. The Joint Report acknowledges that market-to-market

enhancements have been deprioritized compared to reliability considerations: “These efforts will

proceed after the foundational reliability enhancing workstreams described above are established

and operational experience is available.” 3 While the reliability concerns are critical, insufficient

consideration regarding how to realize these economic benefits may result in economic

inefficiency, negatively impacting market participants.

           The Joint Report acknowledges that the West currently lacks a mechanism for

coordinating least-cost redispatch across multiple organized markets. 4 Therefore, when a

constraint affects both market areas, one market may dispatch higher-cost resources despite a

lower-cost solution existing across the market boundary. CAISO and SPP identify this as an

efficiency issue and note that the Eastern Interconnection has measures in place to address such

inefficiencies, but note that “implementing such a system in the West will require substantial

work.” 5 CAISO and SPP also recognize that “equitable attribution and allocation of redispatch

cost for loop flows remains an open issue across the Western Interconnection,” and that

 economic equity will be more closely evaluated as operational experience progresses. 6 The

Parties also note that they will be submitting a seams coordination agreement to the Commission

with an effective date of October 1, 2027, but it will only memorialize the near-term objectives

detailed in the Joint Report, and will not address the broader issues related to market-to-market

economic seams impacts. 7 In general, the Parties appear aware of the potential for economic

inefficiency arising during cross-seams trade, but do not explicitly identify issues that are likely

to materialize and do not set a timeline for addressing these issues.

            For example, the Joint Report almost exclusively considers costs in relation to congestion

management, neglecting to incorporate discussion of possible wheeling fees, price visibility, and

gaps or differences in transmission modeling that result in economic inefficiencies. Transmission

modeling was addressed in the Joint Report, but the focus was placed on congestion management

rather than addressing how transmission modeling differences may limit the ability to trade

across markets. 8 Although the Joint Report extensively discusses operational coordination, it

provides comparatively little analysis of economic barriers that may inhibit efficient trade

between markets.

            Further discussion is necessary regarding economic inefficiencies such as economic

congestion and coordinated dispatch. SPP has discussed the market design of import and export

interchange transactions via the Markets+ Seams Working Group. 9 It is not clear whether parallel

discussions are occurring within CAISO and the EDAM, or whether the Parties are discussing

 this issue in a coordinated manner to avoid negative market outcomes once both markets are

operational.


            b. The Need for Cooperation is Exacerbated by Current Market Conditions

            As discussed above, the Joint Report does not adequately address the potential for

economic friction and the likely inefficiencies resulting from market-to-market coordination and

resource dispatch. The need for this type of close coordination and planning to address these

seams issues would be important under ordinary market conditions, but the current overheated

conditions of the electricity markets place even more importance on proactive measures to avoid

negative customer outcomes.

            The grid is in a state of rapid development that has not been seen in decades. Demand

growth driven by new large loads, electrification of transportation and heating, and other factors

are leading to significant buildouts of new generating capacity and new transmission. This trend

is being acutely felt in the Western Interconnection, with large growth in infrastructure

investments forecasted in the coming years.

            Earlier this year, the Western Transmission Expansion Coalition (WestTEC) published the

results of its 10-year report on needed grid expansion. 10 The study’s Reference Case analysis

relied largely on standard data sources, including utility planning projections and the Western

Electricity Coordinating Council 2034 Anchor Data Set. The WestTEC Reference Case

forecasted peak load growth of 2.4% per year through 2035, double the rate of the preceding 10

years, and new generation capacity additions of 173 MW (nameplate) by 2035. 11 In addition, the


10
  WestTEC, West-wide Transmission Study:10-Year Horizon Report (Feb. 2026),
https://www.westernpowerpool.org/private-media/documents/WestTEC_10-year_Full_Report.pdf.
11
     Id. at 6–7.

                                                    6
 study found that the region will need over $60 billion in planned or newly identified transmission

investment, including 105 individual projects totaling over 12,000 line-miles. 12 These projections

reflect an historic expansion of infrastructure in a short period of time.

             The unprecedented pace of transmission and generation expansion will pose new

challenges to efficient grid management, and places increased emphasis on the value of avoiding

economic inefficiency. While it is unknown precisely how system evolution will impact

customers in specific markets, it is likely that there will be inefficiencies related to congestion

and the differences in market rules between EDAM and Markets+.

             As discussed below, the Parties have suggested a reactive approach to addressing

economic seams issues. 13 During a period of rapid infrastructure development, this strategy is

likely to be continually lagging behind market conditions. Customer interests would be better

served by proactively identifying and managing seams issues to avoid compounding risks.

             c. Markets Present Overlapping Footprints Which May Generate Seams Costs

             Based on current market participation, EDAM and Markets+ present significantly

overlapping footprints, as demonstrated in Figure 1 below. This overlap highlights the market

footprints of participating balancing authorities, as well as the transmission pathways connecting

the geographically scattered footprints of each market.

13

           In the context of these overlapping footprints, trade between markets may cross seams

multiple times. Consider a trade from the Pacific Northwest to a balancing authority area (BAA)

in the desert Southwest. In this scenario, the trade may pass through both markets, in addition to

non-participating, third-party BAAs. Misalignment of any import, export, or wheel-through

charges may significantly impact the economics of certain contract paths. In this situation,

inefficiencies and costs would compound across each seam, inhibiting trade that might be

otherwise efficient. This could impact existing supply contracts or future arrangements.

           FERC has further identified overlapping transmission ownership and rights as an area of

concern. 16 This concern is particularly relevant for any interregional transmission that would

 connect the two markets. The Parties note that transmission service will ultimately be

administered under existing Transmission Service Provider tariff, and that neither market would

create new transmission rights nor expand the physical scheduling authority of transmission

           The specific issues that may arise from these overlapping footprints are numerous. While

it is impossible to anticipate all seams issues with perfect foresight, the Parties have not

sufficiently discussed the extent to which overlapping market footprints may impact seams trade,

nor the extent to which they have considered these issues to-date.


           d. Shifting Participation and New Market Entrants May Generate Additional
              Seams Costs

           The simultaneous development of two competing markets in the same large geographic

footprint presents a unique and challenging circumstance for seams management, and is a

challenge that has not been addressed by the Parties in the Joint Report. The locations of seams

today may differ substantially from those that exist in the future, and the borders between

markets will continue to evolve as utilities and BAAs make decisions regarding market

participation. Even once initial membership decisions are made, seams issues could continue to

evolve as new participants join a market or existing participants switch market alignment.

           For example, while the Bonneville Power Administration initially committed to

Markets+, it recently indicated its intent to participate in EDAM instead. 18 Idaho Power has also

indicated its interest in joining EDAM on top of its existing involvement in the Western Energy

18

                                                        9
 Imbalance Market. If Idaho Power joins EDAM, that could pull a significant portion of Idaho’s

load and transmission capability into the EDAM footprint, affecting where the seam between

EDAM and Markets+ ultimately falls. 19 While these examples do not necessarily guarantee

future volatility in market participation, they illustrate the potential for these seams to shift over

time. In the context of already overlapping market footprints, shifting seams may significantly

impact the magnitude and location of seams inefficiencies, while increasing the associated

uncertainty.

        The Joint Report does not discuss the impact of shifting seams, nor does it consider

potential pathways to mitigate these impacts. New market entrants and the potential for shifting

commitments are an ever-present risk that may not be entirely mitigable. However, proactive

consideration of this risk could result in coordination processes that minimize negative

externalities to other market participants. Further consideration of this market integration process

should be provided prior to the implementation of Markets+.


        e. Effective Cooperation Requires a Concrete Plan for Coordination

        The Joint Report outlines six near-term objectives for CAISO and SPP: 1) education and

training, 2) data sharing, 3) model alignment, 4) implementation of the Western Interconnection

Loading Relief and the Enhanced Curtailment Calculator, 5) development of a framework for

jointly impacted constraint management, and 6) publishing a longer-term plan for seams

coordination. Many of the near-term priorities reflect the continuation of processes that existed

prior to market development efforts.

            While the Parties demonstrate an intent to continue coordination across seams, they have

not established a concrete plan to identify and address various seams issues that may arise. In

essence, the Parties intend to address seams issues as they arise rather than beforehand. In the

near-term, the Parties intend to negotiate and file a seams coordination agreement limited to the

six objectives outlined above, acknowledging that a variety of issues may not be addressed prior

to Markets+ implementation. 20

           CEBA appreciates that there are multiple uncertain elements as well as characteristics

unique to the Western Interconnection which may inhibit the Parties’ ability to completely

mitigate seams impacts proactively. However, these conditions do not absolve the Parties from

considering or mitigating any reasonably addressable seams impacts. Indeed, FERC concluded

that “entities in the West can derive reliability, congestion management, and economic efficiency

benefits by taking proactive steps to coordinate operations….” 21

           The Joint Report has insufficiently considered these economic interactions between the

markets. The Commission should consider requiring a future filing, prior to the implementation

of Markets+, wherein the Parties outline the key economic inefficiencies that may arise at market

seams. This potential filing should also provide a timeline under which these issues would be

addressed, the fora through which they will be discussed, and consideration of the appropriate

agreements that might mitigate those inefficiencies.

            f. Eastern Interconnection Market Experiences Can Inform Coordination in the
              West

           Multiple parties have acknowledged that market development in the Eastern

Interconnection can be instructional for EDAM and Markets+. FERC Staff particularly has

provided a detailed assessment of the development of eastern markets, highlighting a variety of

seams coordination mechanisms including joint operating agreements, congestion management

agreements, interregional market transaction processes, and other seams coordination

agreements. 22

           The entities in the Eastern Interconnection have spent over two decades navigating

interactions and governance issues across multiple regional transmission organizations and

independent system operators (RTOs/ISOs). Many of the challenges facing EDAM and Markets+

have direct Eastern analogues. For example, prior to market-to-market coordination, energy

dispatch decisions between the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) and PJM

Interconnection (PJM) would cause uncompensated congestion or reliability issues in the

adjacent network. 23 The 2004 Joint Operating Agreement between MISO and PJM laid the

operational groundwork for market-to-market coordination and the Congestion Management

Process. This agreement allowed both RTOs to jointly dispatch generation to solve physical

transmission constraints along the seam in the most economically efficient way possible.

           The Eastern Interconnection also utilizes Coordinated Transaction Scheduling (CTS) to

economically coordinate transactions across borders separately from reliability or operational

agreements. Such agreements exist between PJM and MISO, PJM and the New York



22
     Staff White Paper at 10–11.
23
     MISO, Prepared Remarks of Melissa Seymour, Docket No. AD19-13-000, at 7 (filed July 3, 2019).

                                                        12
 Independent System Operator (NYISO), and NYISO and ISO New England . CTS looks at

interface bids using market data from both regions and schedules interchange transactions on 15-

minute intervals (shortly before real time). 24 CTS can also be a cautionary tale: at the end of

2026, MISO and PJM will retire their CTS product as it was not economically beneficial enough

to justify the cost of software maintenance. This may also serve as a lesson for the West in

considering the infrastructure and long-term benefits of such systems. 25

           The Western Interconnection presents certain unique characteristics from its Eastern

counterpart. For example, the Western Interconnection spans multiple BAAs, market operators,

transmission service providers, government entities, and other actors across multiple Open

Access Transmission Tariffs and market protocols. Many of these entities will remain

autonomous, inhibiting centralized operations in the same manner exhibited in the Eastern

Interconnection. Indeed, the final set of seams coordination mechanisms will not be identical to

those in the Eastern Interconnection.

           Nonetheless, mechanisms like CTS should be high-priority areas for market-to-market

coordination prior to market implementation. Given the Parties’ acknowledgement that such an

issue “will necessitate a staged, carefully coordinated approach,” it is unclear why such a seams

mitigation measure is not highlighted as a near-term priority. 26 The Commission should consider

directing a future filing wherein the Parties provide further discussion of how learnings from the

Eastern Interconnection can inform the seams coordination.

 III.   CONCLUSION

       CEBA appreciates the Parties’ status update regarding the development of EDAM and

Markets+, particularly regarding the various coordination activities taking place between the

Parties. The Parties need to approach seams coordination with the necessary rigor, and working

toward developing coordination mechanisms that will mitigate any negative externalities to

market participants and the broader Western Interconnection.

       However, the Parties have not demonstrated a holistic consideration of the various

inefficiencies that may materialize across seams. Particularly, the Joint Report does not

sufficiently consider economic friction that is likely to occur at seams, nor how overlapping and

shifting seams may exacerbate these inefficiencies. Absent a concrete process through which the

Parties identify such risks and develop pathways to appropriate mitigation, it is likely that market

participants and consumers will be negatively impacted. To this end, CEBA recommends that the

Commission require the Parties to file a supplement to the Joint Report addressing economic

inefficiencies at seams, the impacts of overlapping and shifting seams, and the specific process

through which the Parties intend to identify and mitigate known inefficiencies that are likely to

materialize during cross-seam trade. In the alternative, CEBA recommends that the Commission

establish a mandatory schedule for additional filings from the Parties after both markets are in

operation.
